articles.title: Characterisation of human hair follicle development.
articles.authors: Zoe R Sudderick, James D Glover, Cameron Batho-Samblas et al.
articles.abstract: Humans have a characteristic distribution of hair across the body. Visible, relatively long and thick terminal hair fibres are present on the scalp and eyebrows in childhood, and are stimulated to grow on other parts of the body, such as the beard and armpits, by hormones during puberty. The short and fine vellus hairs, in contrast, are not readily visible and cover most of the body, including the face. Here we report quantification of the timing and characteristics of hair follicle development in human embryogenesis, from gestational Weeks 8-19, and compare this to mouse hair follicle development. We find that human hair follicles develop first on the head, where we identify several distinct initiation sites, followed by the torso. Clustered follicular units are produced by secondary hair follicles budding off the epidermis from sites close to earlier-forming primary follicles. Arrector pili muscles are detected from gestational Week 17. Although terminal and vellus hair follicles have clear differences in the adult, both hair types initially develop from placodes and dermal condensates of similar size. Once their development is initiated, we find that human hair follicles grow and mature at the same rate, regardless of anatomical location, but have different density at different body sites. These findings demonstrate that regional differences in hair characteristics of human skin, such as the distinction between scalp and forehead, are largely caused by processes that act after the initial stages of hair follicle morphogenesis. Efforts to understand the evolution of human 'hairlessness' should, therefore, focus on genetic and cellular events that take place after hair follicle morphogenesis. We compared human skin appendages, including eccrine sweat glands, with those in mouse. We found that molecular markers, such as EDA, EDAR, SOX2 and WNT pathway components, are broadly similar in expression between both species, although species-specific differences do exist. Notably, SOX2 expression, which distinguishes different hair follicle types in the mouse, is detected in all human hair follicle types, though with a later onset of expression than that observed in mouse. Together with comparison of morphology and gene expression, these results support the use of embryonic mouse primary hair follicles as a model for human hair follicle development.

articles.title: Allometric patterns in Rhamphorhynchus muensteri and their role in the paleoecology, life habits, and taxonomic framework of pterosaurs.
articles.authors: Gabriela Menezes Cerqueira, João Lucas Da Silva, Ingmar Werneburg et al.
articles.abstract: Pterosaurs were the first vertebrates to achieve powered flight, a result of various unique anatomical adaptations, and significant morphological diversity throughout their evolutionary history. Although the pterosaurs body structure was specialized for powered flight, the clade exhibited great disparity from its origins, with later evolution giving rise to multiple phylogenetic lineages and a wide range of body sizes, from small forms such as Anurognathus ammoni to truly giant species like Quetzalcoatlus northropi. This variation led to distinct flight strategies within the group. Here, we assess allometry in the skeletal elements of Rhamphorhynchus muensteri in comparison with Eupterodactyloidea and Euctenochasmatia, examining their implications for paleoecology and flight capacity. The analysis included 127 specimens and assessed 13 skeletal variables using statistical methods, principal components analysis (PCA), and standardized major analysis (SMA). The results reveal differences in size-shape trajectories and functional adaptations related to activity flight. R. muensteri exhibits a trend of negative allometry (PCRW/body, humerus, radius/ulna, metacarpal IV, and femur), indicating distinct allometric scaling patterns and flight style. These patterns suggest behavior and ecological differences, as well differing flight capabilities between R. muensteri likely relied on active flapping flight interspersed with gliding, whereas other taxa may have exhibited greater migratory adaptations within Eupterodactyloidea, and a greater dependence on flapping flight in Euctenochasmatia. The negative allometry in R. muensteri suggests a flight style characterized by early flight capability (precocial flight), whereas Eupterodactyloidea showed positive allometry and Euctenochasmatia isometry. Additionally, the study highlights how allometric patterns influence pterosaur phylogeny, underscoring the importance of incorporating them into future analysis.

articles.title: Scratching beneath the surface: Quantification of muscle architecture and myosin heavy chain content in the forelimbs of black-tailed prairie dogs (Cynomys, Rodentia).
articles.authors: Luke A Scheetz, Carter A Burnett, Benjamin R Kimble et al.
articles.abstract: Black-tailed prairie dogs (Cynomys ludovicianus) excavate burrow systems for a variety of reasons, including social organization and predator avoidance. As such, they have evolved a suite of musculoskeletal traits in their forelimbs that are employed for scratch-digging (i.e., digging motion performed by alternating power and recovery strokes). However, the degree to which their muscular anatomy has become modified in response to the selective pressures of their semi-fossorial lifestyle is unknown. To better understand the functional capacities of their forelimb musculature, dissections of C. ludovicianus (N = 9) were conducted to quantify limb mechanical advantage, muscle architectural properties, and myosin heavy chain (MHC) isoform content. Compared with previous data from other ground squirrels, forelimb muscle mass distribution in black-tailed prairie dogs is broadly similar with a large investment of scapular and shoulder muscle mass that accounts for two-thirds of the total forelimb muscle mass. The majority of muscles have long fascicles with correspondingly high fascicle length-to-muscle length (LF/ML) ratios, whereas aside from the main carpal and digital flexors/extensors, selected intrinsic shoulder flexors/extensors, and the smallest elbow extensors, most muscles have low physiological cross-sectional area to muscle mass (PCSA/MM) ratios. Notably, only the massive m. pectoralis superficialis was considered to be a high power muscle by its architectural properties, although several muscles are modified for large joint torque or torque range, including m. latissimus dorsi and a well-developed m. triceps brachii long head. Mechanical advantage is correspondingly greatest at the shoulder joint, intermediate at the elbow joint, and low at the carpal joint. Lastly, muscle composition is fast-contracting by moderate expression of fast MHC-2B and low expression of slow MHC-1. That said, %MHC isoform content shows a predominance of fast MHC-2A as predicted, which progressively increases distally throughout the forelimb. These findings collectively suggest that C. ludovicianus is less specialized among burrowing rodents as hypothesized. Its forelimb musculoskeletal properties are likely constrained by a preference for medium soil types and cooperative social behavior, and may further represent a trade-off between terrestrial locomotor behavior and digging function. Nonetheless, the modifications observed are comparible with other semi-fossorial members of the Marmotini tribe with respect to distinctive traits for scratch-digging. Future work is needed to quantify muscle properties in additional genera (e.g., Tamias, Spermophilus) to better assess selection for burrowing in ground squirrels.

articles.title: The variability of giraffe skull morphology.
articles.authors: Nikolaos Kargopoulos, Jesús Marugán-Lobón, Anusuya Chinsamy-Turan et al.
articles.abstract: Giraffe (Giraffa spp.) are among the most unique and charismatic extant animals, largely due to their distinct morphology. The evolutionary and developmental origin of ossicones is a key factor in giraffid biology, yet other features building their characteristic head physiognomy remain poorly studied. Here, we analysed the cranial diversity of extant Giraffa using a continent-wide sample with a balanced sex ratio and ontogenetic growth series, using shape analysis (3D geometric morphometrics). Detailed comparisons showed significant differences in cranial morphology across the four Giraffa species, and in some cases also between subspecies of the same species. The analyses revealed that females reach adult cranial form at an earlier age (around 4 years old), while males continue growing until the eighth year, aligning with the onset of sexual maturity for each of the sexes. Multivariate methods unambiguously prompt significant covariation between skull parts. Such high covariation patterns indicate that Giraffa skull morphology largely evolves as a whole (i.e., morphologically integrated), even though parts of it (such as the ossicones) develop in different magnitudes. Considering their role in territorial and mating behaviours, we suggest that ossicone morphology influences the parapatric evolution of Giraffa through sexual selection. Palaeontological evidence shows that development of larger ossicones is a relatively recent trait for members of the genus Giraffa, with the cranial morphology of the southern giraffe (Giraffa giraffa) being the closest to that of the ancestral forms, possibly through plesiomorphy or paedomorphosis.

articles.title: Comparative histological analysis of vertebrates reveals Triassic climate variability across southern Pangea.
articles.authors: Valerie Trinidad, Darlington Munyikwa, Michel Zondo et al.
articles.abstract: Climate highly influenced the distribution of major animal groups that emerged during the Triassic throughout the supercontinent Pangea. The earliest dinosaurs and associated assemblages (Carnian Stage, Late Triassic, ~230 Ma) are recovered along a paleolatitudinal climate belt spanning southern Pangea. However, developmental responses of different amniotic clades to climate across these environments remain unknown. Characterizing developmental variability, presumably driven in part by climatic variability within this belt, helps constrain the climatic ranges that shaped the earliest dinosaurs prior to their worldwide dispersal, while also providing insights into developmental plasticity of Triassic fauna. We analyzed the bone histology of five vertebrate taxa from the Carnian of Zimbabwe, including sauropodomorph and herrerasaurid dinosaurs, a gomphodontosuchine cynodont, a hyperodapedontine rhynchosaur, and a suchian archosaur (?aetosaur) as a proxy to assess probable climatic influence by comparing various growth strategies/metabolisms of these clades across southern Pangea. The dinosaurs are continuously growing individuals that exhibit well-vascularized woven-parallel and parallel-fibered cortical bone with no apparent growth marks. The cynodont is an immature specimen with a well-vascularized fibrolamellar matrix that has anastomosing vascular canals throughout the cortex and a single growth mark, indicating rapid growth. The rhynchosaurian femur and suchian tibia show moderate to poorly vascularized parallel-fibered and woven-fibered matrixes possessing multiple lines of arrested growth along with an external fundamental system, suggesting these were slow-growing individuals that had reached skeletal maturity at the time of death. Comparing this histology to that of similar assemblages from current-day Brazil, Argentina, and India (which fell along the same paleolatitudinal zone during the Triassic), the mid-continent (i.e., Zimbabwean) dinosaurs exhibit continuous uninterrupted growth in contrast to other histologically sampled dinosaurs from different localities along this climatic belt, whereas the Zimbabwean rhynchosaur and suchian exhibit patterns with more frequent cessation of growth than their South American counterparts. Slower-growing Zimbabwean taxa-presumably, more susceptible to climatic stressors-exhibit characteristics suggestive of a less resource-rich environment (e.g., frequent cessations, more interrupted growth) compared with rhynchosaurs and aetosaurs from South America. Taxa with faster growth rates and higher metabolic regimes (i.e., dinosaurs, cynodont) from this same assemblage apparently grew rapidly-and roughly continuously-throughout the year. This is consistent with an overall more arid but less seasonal climate in Zimbabwe compared to the signals recovered in Brazil, Argentina, and India.

articles.title: A statistical shape model of the human female sacrum: An integrative analysis of form.
articles.authors: Liesbeth Van Hauwermeiren, Emmanuel Audenaert, Jan Van Houcke et al.
articles.abstract: Sacral shape has been investigated in the context of many disciplines, such as anthropology, forensics and in clinical contexts. The female population is of special interest, given the complex interaction between locomotor, thermoregulatory and obstetric demands on the pelvis. However, interpretation of results between current studies is limited by the use of a diverse range of parameters, often offering an oversimplified and fragmented view on sacral shape. We investigated sacral shape in a young adult female population between 18 and 40 years old, using a statistical shape model based on 109 3D CT datasets and principal component analysis. This study provides a comprehensive and visually intuitive view on sacral shape, describing general shape patterns and covariation between different regions of the sacrum. Two dominant shape components were sacral size and sagittal curvature. Both components were associated with specific shape variations in the load-bearing areas of the sacrum, indicating a relationship between shape and function. This study generates hypotheses on sacral shape and its relation to function that warrant further research.

articles.title: Descriptive, comparative, and functional anatomy of the facial musculature in cattle (Bos taurus).
articles.authors: Maja Söderlind, Bridget Cain, Katrina Ask et al.
articles.abstract: Facial expressions can provide insight into animal emotions and pain, but no standardized system for assessing the entire facial display in cattle (Bos taurus Linnaeus) exists. The Facial Action Coding System (FACS), originally developed for humans, identifies distinct facial movements based on mimetic muscles. Developing a cattle-specific FACS requires mapping and comparing cattle mimetic musculature with that of humans and related species, which was the aim of this study. Dissection of three heads-using skinning and facial mask preparation on opposite sides-identified 30 mimetic muscles and revealed notable fiber blending in the lower face and ear region. The method helped clarify subtle anatomical discrepancies in previous literature that are important for interpreting muscle function. Muscular differences with humans and horses suggest a slightly less diverse or different facial repertoire in cattle. Robust lips and a different lip-muscle arrangement likely restrict the marginal, upper lip, and lip-corner movements described in one or both comparison species. A broad insertion of the M. levator labii superioris indicates involvement in both upper lip and nostril movements, and several muscles appeared to influence nostril shape. The eyebrow region-served only by a broad M. frontalis-suggests fewer eyebrow movements than in humans and broader ones than in horses. Cattle also possess musculature supporting movements not described in one or both comparison species, including upper lip retraction, nostril lifting, cheek raising, and diverse ear movements supported by well-developed ear muscles. The findings provide a basis for developing a FACS for cattle, pending validation in live animals.

articles.title: Hominin postcranial remains from Drimolen Main Quarry, South Africa.
articles.authors: Caley M Orr, Stephanie E Baker, Tara E Hobbs et al.
articles.abstract: Drimolen Main Quarry (the primary excavation within the Drimolen paleocave system in Gauteng Province, South Africa) dates to ~2 Ma and has yielded abundant hominin remains. Most craniodental specimens are attributed to Paranthropus robustus, but the collection also includes a cranial vault of Homo aff. erectus and teeth with early Homo affinities. Here we catalog isolated postcranial specimens recovered between 1994 and 2015 and contribute formal descriptions along with comparative and functional analyses to provide further information on the paleobiology of the Drimolen hominins. Twenty-eight fossil specimens are cataloged, although two previously considered as possibly hominin are formally removed from that status. Like the craniodental assemblage, the postcrania include a high proportion of juveniles and subadults. Upper limb elements include an adult distal humerus (DNH 32), ulnar fragment (DNH 109, previously described), three fetal/perinatal humeri, three fetal/perinatal radius fragments, and nine manual phalanges. Lower limb elements include two fetal/perinatal tibiae, hallucal metatarsal, and nonhallucal pedal proximal phalanx. Vertebral and pelvic material include an adult lumbar centrum, a partial pelvis (DNH 43, previously described), and infant thoracic and lumbar neural arches (DNH 150 a and b). DNH 32 and DNH 43 can be attributed to P. robustus with some confidence while DNH 150a and b can possibly be associated with the DNH 134 juvenile cranium attributed to Homo aff. erectus. Although most other specimens probably belong to P. robustus, taxonomic attribution is challenging given Drimolen's mixed assemblage. Functional analyses indicate small-bodied hominins committed to terrestrial bipedality. However, the first metatarsal evinces a tight tarsometatarsal joint curvature possibly suggesting increased hallucal divergence in that individual. These results might reflect taxonomic variation or evolutionary mosaicism of the postcrania.

articles.title: Comparative cranial biomechanics reveal macroevolutionary trends in theropod dinosaurs, with emphasis on Tyrannosauroidea.
articles.authors: Evan Johnson-Ransom, Paul Gignac, Daniel E Barta et al.
articles.abstract: Tyrannosaurus is viewed as a model organism in vertebrate paleontology, with numerous studies analyzing its feeding biomechanics. Nonetheless, the evolution of this feeding performance has been under-addressed in Tyrannosauroidea, especially in basal tyrannosauroids. Here we used muscle-force reconstruction and finite element analysis (FEA) to quantify the cranial performance of tyrannosauroids and outgroup theropod clades. 2D (planar) cranial models, set to standardized skull lengths and jaw adductor forces, were used to analyze the evolution of feeding behavior in a large sample size of Tyrannosauroidea and other theropods. Sampled stresses matched well between planar and 3D analyses of three disparately shaped crania, suggesting valid interpretations from 2D models along the lateral sides of theropod crania if symmetrical bite loadings are assumed. We traced cranial evolution by sampling stresses at homologous points of theropod crania and input their average stress values into a maximum likelihood ancestral character state estimation. Our results show tyrannosauroids having moderate-to-low cranial stresses. We further tested whether the average stress value correlates with head size through phylogenetic generalized least square regressions. We found that 2D FEA provides significant information on the evolution of feeding performance in a major dinosaur clade. Along internal branches of Tyrannosauroidea, hypothetical common ancestors exhibit low cranial stress values owing to a combination of robust skulls and cranial protuberances. These traits may have been passed down to later tyrannosauroids, enabling them to handle high forces. Our results additionally demonstrate a possible correlation between cranial shape (brevirostrine versus longirostrine) and inferred cranial performance in non-tyrannosauroid clades.

articles.title: Osteohistology of two phorusrhacids reveals uninterrupted growth strategy.
articles.authors: Lotta Dreyer, Christian Cooper, Jingmai O'Connor
articles.abstract: Phorusrhacidae were apex predators that primarily dominated South America ecosystems for at least 40 million years with their imposing size and predatory lifestyle-yet some aspects of their biology remain poorly understood. Osteohistology is a tool for understanding growth dynamics and biomechanical adaptations. Despite their ecological significance, histological analyses of these birds were non-existent until the recent publication of a sampled metatarsus. Here, we present the first osteohistological data of a phorusrhacid femur together with other hindlimb elements representing two taxa, Andrewsornis abbotti and Physornis fortis, from the late Oligocene of Argentina. Ground-section microscopy reveals highly vascularized fibrolamellar bone tissue, indicating rapid, sustained growth with lines of arrested growth appearing only in the outer circumferential layer. Extensive secondary remodeling, particularly at muscle attachment sites, highlights high mechanical stress, consistent with active cursorial locomotion. Body mass estimates (60-89 kg for Andrewsornis abbotti) and high relative cortical thickness in both specimens (bone compactness = 0.55-0.78) provide additional data for comparative studies. Our findings confirm the uninterrupted growth strategy of phorusrhacids, consistent with other large-bodied flightless neognaths but in contrast to most giant flightless palaeognath birds.

articles.title: Anatomical Network Analyses of Pre- and Post-Metamorphic Cranial Systems Support the Adaptive Decoupling Hypothesis in Anura.
articles.authors: Lorenz Guschker, Maximilian A Stüwe, Hendrik Müller et al.
articles.abstract: Complex life cycles characterized by distinct life phases connected by a metamorphosis raise the question whether traits of these distinct life phases can evolve independently or remain evolutionarily coupled. Because metamorphosis can include trait reorganization between life phases, the adaptive decoupling hypothesis proposes that larval and adult traits may evolve largely independent of each other. In anurans, the cranial system undergoes a major reorganization during metamorphosis, transitioning from a distinct cartilaginous larval cranium to an ossified adult cranium, yet this transformation has never been quantitatively characterized across species. We applied Anatomical Network Analysis (AnNA) to the cranial musculoskeletal systems of larval and adult anurans with different feeding and developmental modes. AnNA describes the topological organization of the cranium without the need for homologous landmarks, allowing comparisons between morphologically disparate systems. We calculated topological parameters describing integration and modularity, as well as connectivity modules (Q-modules) within each cranial network. As part of that analysis, expanded morphological descriptions of the cranial musculoskeletal system of larval and adult Smilisca phaeota were made. Larval and embryonic crania are topologically highly integrated and less modular, whereas adult crania are less integrated and organized into distinct modules. As a result, larval and adult life phases occupy distinct regions within a topological morphospace, whereby larvae and embryos of endotrophic anurans, despite lacking a free-living larval stage, cluster consistently within the larval topological space. Together, these findings support the adaptive decoupling hypothesis for the cranial system across anuran life phases.

articles.title: Intraskeletal Pathway of the Trigeminal Nerve in Modern Bird Beak: 3D Comparative Anatomy Using the diceCT Method.
articles.authors: Noriyuki Wakimizu, Takanobu Tsuihiji
articles.abstract: The morphology of the trigeminal nerve extending through the snout region in Archosauria has recently been the focus of extensive research, particularly in paleontology. However, the pathways of this nerve within cranial bones in extant birds have not been described in detail. Here, we describe trigeminal nerve pathways in the skull of nine avian species using a non-destructive soft-tissue imaging technique (diceCT) with a particular emphasis on osteological correlates, including intraskeletal neurovascular canals as well as foramina and grooves on the bony surfaces. In many species, a branch of the trigeminal nerve, the ophthalmic nerve, extends through the anterior premaxillary canal. Similarly, another branch of the trigeminal nerve, the maxillary nerve, passes through a bony canal in the maxillopalatine process at the posterior end of the snout in many species. However, apparently clade-specific unique pathways are also observed for the ophthalmic nerve around the external naris in Falconiformes and Psittaciformes and the maxillary nerve on the palatal surface in Anseriformes, the latter of which is likely associated with the specialized tactile sensation. Based on comparison with the condition in Crocodylia, the "reptilian-like" course of the maxillary nerve within the premaxilla is considered to have apomorphically been lost, whereas that of the ophthalmic nerve within the premaxilla has become extremely prominent in Aves. These changes in the intraskeletal nerve pathways in Aves have likely been associated with the enlargement of the premaxilla and the loss of teeth in the avialan lineage. The present observation of the trigeminal nerve pathway in Aves potentially contributes to the discussion of the homology of other associated soft-tissue structures and the presence of special sensory functions in fossil archosaurs.

articles.title: Effects of stellate ganglion blockade on pulmonary artery pressure and sympathetic baroreflex function at high altitude: a case study in treated hypertension.
articles.authors: Qudus A Ojikutu, Jenna C McCrone, Christabel Osei-Boateng et al.
articles.abstract: In this case study, we explored whether transient inhibition of sympathetic outflow with stellate ganglion blockade (SGB) modifies pulmonary artery pressure and sympathetic arterial baroreflex regulation during high-altitude (HA) exposure in an individual with treated hypertension. A 44-yr-old man with treated hypertension underwent physiological assessments at sea level (220 m) and after 5-8 days of exposure to HA (3,800 m). Pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PASP), muscle sympathetic nerve activity (MSNA), beat-by-beat blood pressure (BP), carotid artery diameter, and spontaneous sympathetic baroreflex function (integrative and mechanical components) were assessed at sea level and during HA exposure. During HA exposure, these measurements were obtained following a right-sided ultrasound-guided SGB and compared with those obtained in subsequent time-control visits. HA exposure increased PASP, MSNA, BP, and BP variability compared with sea level. SGB reduced PASP, whereas no meaningful change occurred during the time-control visit. BP variability was lower following SGB than during the control visit. The integrative sympathetic arterial baroreflex relationship appeared steeper following SGB, and the mechanical component demonstrated a greater slope than during the time-control visit, consistent with altered mechanical baroreceptor transduction. These observations suggest that regional sympathetic inhibition may exert distinct influences on pulmonary artery pressure and sympathetic baroreflex regulation during sustained high-altitude exposure in treated hypertension.NEW & NOTEWORTHY This physiological case study examined the effects of stellate ganglion blockade (SGB) during sustained high-altitude exposure in an individual with treated hypertension. Unilateral SGB reduced pulmonary artery systolic pressure and was associated with changes in sympathetic arterial baroreflex regulation and carotid pressure-diameter behavior. These observations provide preliminary evidence that regional sympathetic activity may influence pulmonary vascular and carotid mechanical responses during sustained hypoxic exposure.

articles.title: The interaction of surface stiffness and hopping frequency on the metabolic cost and biomechanics of human hopping.
articles.authors: Luis Morata-Moreno, Alena Marie Grabowski
articles.abstract: The use of in-series passive-elastic devices, such as surfaces and shoes, can reduce the metabolic cost of bouncing gaits, such as running and hopping. These reductions in metabolic cost may arise from increased leg stiffness and ground contact time with less stiff surfaces or footwear. We examined how changes in surface stiffness influence the metabolic cost and biomechanics of hopping across a range of frequencies. As changes in hopping frequency result in changes in leg stiffness and ground contact time, we hypothesized that the metabolic cost associated with hopping on elastic surfaces would be modulated by hopping frequency. Sixteen participants hopped in place on both feet at 2.4, 2.6, and 2.8 Hz on surfaces with different linear stiffness (rigid ∼35,000 kN/m, and 0.9, 0.7, and 0.5 kN/m/kg) using a custom-built adjustable elastic springy platform while we collected metabolic, ground-reaction force, and kinematic data. Hopping on elastic surfaces reduced net metabolic power (W/kg) by 17.6-44.7% compared with a rigid surface; however, the surface stiffness that minimized net metabolic power was stiffer at faster hopping frequencies. We also found that leg stiffness and ground contact time increased as surface stiffness decreased, and this effect was amplified at faster hopping frequencies. These biomechanical changes were not consistently associated with net metabolic power changes. Our data suggest that surface energy return was most closely timed with leg extension on stiffer surfaces at faster hopping frequencies. Thus, tuning in-series passive-elastic devices to a user's movement frequency may reduce the metabolic cost of bouncing gaits.NEW & NOTEWORTHY Metabolic cost reductions for stationary hopping on elastic compared with rigid surfaces are frequency dependent. We found that the surface stiffness that minimized metabolic cost was stiffer at faster hopping frequencies. Leg stiffness and contact time increased as surface stiffness decreased, and this effect was amplified at faster hopping frequencies. These findings suggest that the stiffness of passive-elastic devices, like elastic surfaces and footwear, should be tuned to movement frequency to minimize metabolic cost.

articles.title: Cold fluid ingestion does not enhance exogenous carbohydrate oxidation during prolonged endurance exercise in the heat.
articles.authors: Loïs Mougin, Ben Will, Coen C W G Bongers et al.
articles.abstract: This study investigated the effects of ingesting cold versus warm carbohydrate beverages on exogenous carbohydrate oxidation and time-trial performance during prolonged cycling in the heat. Eleven trained, non heat-acclimated cyclists [21 ± 3 yr; 69.3 ± 8.3 kg; peak oxygen uptake ([Formula: see text]): 64.7 ± 5.0 mL/kg/min] completed two trials comprising 100 min of submaximal cycling at 50% Wpeak followed by a time trial in a hot environment (36.2 ± 0.3°C; 55 ± 3% relative humidity). Participants ingested a 15% dextrose solution enriched with [U-13C] glucose (60 g/h; bolus every 20 min) provided either cold (COLD; 4.0 ± 1.6°C) or at room temperature (WARM; 35.8 ± 0.5°C). Heart rate and rectal temperature were lower in COLD than in WARM during the 100-min exercise (P ≤ 0.006), whereas skin temperature did not differ between conditions. Average (40-100 min) exogenous carbohydrate oxidation (COLD: 0.50 ± 0.10 vs. WARM: 0.51 ± 0.10 g/min; P = 0.80), peak exogenous carbohydrate oxidation, total carbohydrate and fat oxidation, and blood glucose, lactate, and insulin concentrations did not differ between trials (all P ≥ 0.34). Sweat losses and body mass changes were unaffected by condition (P ≥ 0.40). Time-trial performance was not different between COLD and WARM (P = 0.38). Despite attenuating cardiovascular and thermal strain, ingesting a cold carbohydrate beverage during exercise in the heat did not enhance exogenous carbohydrate oxidation, substrate utilization, or performance compared with a warm beverage.NEW & NOTEWORTHY This study showed that, despite reducing cardiovascular and thermal strain, ingesting a cold (4°C) versus warm (36°C) carbohydrate beverage did not enhance exogenous carbohydrate oxidation, substrate utilization, or time-trial performance during prolonged cycling in the heat. These findings suggest that beverage temperature is not a relevant factor for optimizing carbohydrate availability during exercise under heat stress, and that athletes can select beverage temperature based on palatability and preference rather than for metabolic benefit.

articles.title: Skeletal muscle oxidative capacity and tissue composition in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction.
articles.authors: Miles F Bartlett, Jimin Ren, Satyam Sarma et al.
articles.abstract: Increasing evidence suggests that exercise intolerance in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is related to peripheral abnormalities; however, the roles of muscle oxidative capacity and muscle steatosis remain incompletely understood. To address this knowledge gap, 38 HFpEF patients [mean age 69.8 ± 6.1 yr, body mass index (BMI) 37.6 ± 6.9 kg/m2] and 17 healthy older adults (HOAs; mean age 67.6 ± 5.4 yr, BMI 27.3 ± 4.8 kg/m2) performed a graded exercise test on a cycle ergometer to assess exercise tolerance (peak watts) and whole body aerobic capacity [peak O2 uptake (V̇o2peak)]. In vivo quadriceps oxidative capacity [phosphocreatine recovery time constant (τPCr)] and thigh tissue composition [i.e., lean thigh mass (LTM); intermuscular fat % (IMF%)] were measured separately via 31P-magnetic resonance spectroscopy (31P-MRS) and T2-weighted MRI, respectively. LTM was similar between HFpEF patients and HOAs (P = 0.854), but IMF% was significantly greater in HFpEF (P ≤ 0.001). Peak watts and V̇o2peak normalized to LTM were lower and quadriceps τPCr was slower in HFpEF patients compared to HOAs (all P < 0.03). Although IMF% was associated with peak watts normalized to LTM (R2 = 0.148) and whole body V̇o2peak normalized to body mass (R2 = 0.347), it was not associated with V̇o2peak normalized to LTM (R2 < 0.001) or τPCr (R2 = 0.020). In contrast, V̇o2peak normalized to LTM and quadriceps τPCr were both associated with peak watts (R2 = 0.509 and 0.252, respectively) and with each other (R2 = 0.298). Taken together, these data suggest that exercise intolerance in HFpEF is associated with increased muscle steatosis and impaired whole body and quadriceps muscle oxidative capacity. However, the lack of association between IMF% and measures of oxidative capacity suggest that they affect exercise tolerance via different physiological mechanisms.NEW & NOTEWORTHY We compared peripheral mechanisms of exercise intolerance in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) patients and healthy older adults. HFpEF patients exhibited significantly greater intermuscular steatosis and impaired whole body and quadriceps oxidative capacity [i.e., peak O2 uptake (V̇o2peak) and phosphocreatine recovery time constant (τPCr), respectively], all of which were associated with impaired exercise tolerance. However, increased intermuscular steatosis was not associated with impaired V̇o2peak and τPCr, suggesting that steatosis and impaired oxidative capacity affect exercise tolerance through different physiological mechanisms.

articles.title: Physical Activity Levels and Lung-Kidney Function in a Cohort of COVID-19 Survivors.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.authors: Heitor S Ribeiro, Dário R Mondini, Francisco Z Mattedi et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The relationship between physical activity levels and overall health among survivors of moderate to severe COVID-19 remains underexplored in target organs, such as lungs and kidneys. We examined the association between physical activity levels and lung-kidney abnormalities in survivors of COVID-19 hospitalization. METHODS: A cross-sectional analysis was performed within a prospective cohort of survivors of COVID-19 hospitalization. Physical activity levels were assessed with the International Physical Activity Questionnaire (short form), and physical inactivity was classified according to the World Health Organization guidelines (<150 min/week of physical activity). Abnormal kidney function was defined as estimated glomerular filtration rate <60 mL/min/1.73 m2, whereas pulmonary involvement was defined as chest X-ray pulmonary lesion, and/or forced vital capacity less than the lower limit of normal, and/or altered oximetry. RESULTS: In total, 653 survivors (46% female and 28% ≥65 years) were assessed 8 ± 2 months posthospital discharge. Physical inactivity was found in 53% of the cohort. Lung and kidney abnormalities were observed in 36% and 20% of survivors, respectively, whereas coexistence was observed in 7%. Physically active survivors had lower odds of lung abnormality (32% vs 41%; adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 0.67, 95% confidence interval [CI]:0.47 to 0.97), but not of kidney (17% vs 23%; aOR = 0.81, 95% CI: 0.52 to 1.26) nor lung-kidney abnormality (6% vs 9%; aOR = 0.58, 95% CI: 0.29 to 1.20), compared with those physically inactive. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses showed distinct associations for lung abnormalities by age and among survivors without severe oxygen desaturation or very low kidney function. The restricted cubic spline curve for lung-kidney abnormalities showed a nonlinear dose-response relationship, with higher odds below and lower odds above 150 min/week. CONCLUSIONS: Among survivors of COVID-19 hospitalization, being physically active was associated with better lung function outcomes, but not kidney or composite outcomes. This association was modified by age and baseline clinical status and followed a non-linear dose-response pattern.

articles.title: Determinants of Reclassification of Exercise Performance across Cardiopulmonary Exercise Testing Prediction Equations.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.authors: Faezeh Abbaspour Kaboudan, Siyang Zeng, Yorusaliem Abrham et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Volume of oxygen uptake at peak exercise ( ) is a key indicator of cardiorespiratory fitness used to assess surgical risk and clinical trial outcomes. However, multiple prediction equations exist for its interpretation, often yielding inconsistent classifications of exercise performance. We aimed to determine how different prediction equations affect exercise performance classification and identify factors contributing to its variability. METHODS: We performed a post hoc analysis of cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) data collected from 332 nonsmoking flight attendants who participated in our previous studies examining the health effects of occupational exposure to secondhand tobacco smoke. Percent-predicted was calculated using seven prediction equations (Fitness Registry and the Importance of Exercise National Database, Wasserman, Hansen-Wasserman, Study of Health in Pomerania, Jones, Bruce, and Cooper-Storer). Reduced exercise performance was defined as < 80 percent-predicted. Agreement across equations was assessed using Cohen's κ. Associations with dyspnea (modified Medical Research Council ≥ 1) were examined using C-statistics to assess the discriminative performance of prediction equations for this patient-centered outcome. The magnitude of change in percent-predicted when switching from one equation to another ("recalculation magnitude") was quantified for individual participants, and multivariable regression modeling was used to identify demographic and anthropometric determinants of recalculation magnitude. RESULTS: Participants were 56 ± 12 years old, 86% female, with body mass index = 24 ± 4 kg/m 2 . Depending on the prediction equation, mean percent-predicted varied widely (83%-113%), and the prevalence of reduced exercise performance ranged from 7% to 51%. Agreement across equations ranged from slight to substantial (κ = 0.10-0.79). At an individual level, switching between equations recalculated percent-predicted by -93% to +84%, leading to bidirectional exercise performance reclassification of 6.6%-45.5% of participants. Body mass index was the strongest determinant of recalculation magnitude, followed by age and sex. The discrimination accuracy of prediction equations for dyspnea was modest (area under the curve = 0.56-0.71), with the Study of Health in Pomerania equation showing the best performance. CONCLUSIONS: Different prediction equations yielded materially different percent-predicted values and frequently changed exercise capacity classification in a bidirectional manner. The observed discordance appears to arise in substantial part from limitations in how demographic and anthropometric factors, particularly body size, are modeled across equations, underscoring the need for improved reference standards that better capture physiological variability.

articles.title: Resting Metabolic Rate in Collegiate Male Wrestlers: Cross-Validation and Development of Prediction Equations.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.authors: Andrew R Jagim, Ward C Dobbs, Meghan K Magee et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: The purpose of the current study was to cross-validate previously developed resting metabolic rate (RMR) prediction equations using laboratory measurements of RMR as a criterion. METHODS: National Collegiate Athletic Association Division I (n = 60) and III (n = 113) male wrestlers participated in the current study (n = 173; Age: 19.6 ± 1.5 yrs.; Height: 176.3 ± 6.3 cm; Weight: 76.6 ± 10.9 kg; Body Fat: 11.4 ± 3.0%). Indirect calorimetry was used to measure RMR and Skinfold thickness was used to estimate body fat percentage (BF%) during the preseason period under standardized dress (underwear only), fasting, and resting conditions. RESULTS: Mean measured RMR was 2102 ± 341 kcal·d -1 . All body mass-based RMR prediction equations significantly underestimated the measured RMR, with the exception of the Jagim and Schofield equations. The Tinsley fat-free mass (FFM) equation and the Cunningham equation had the lowest constant error values when compared with measured RMR (mean bias ± standard error: 80 ± 20 kcal and 126 ± 20 kcal·d -1 , respectively). Linear regression indicated the Tinsley FFM (R 2 = 0.422, root-mean-squared error (RMSE) = 279 kcals, %RMSE = 13.3%), and Cunningham FFM equations had the closest agreement to measured RMR (R 2 = 0.422, RMSE = 301 kcals, %RMSE = 14.3%), along with the Jagim equation for a body mass-based prediction equation (R 2 = 0.377, RMSE = 338 kcals, %RMSE = 16.1%). The standard error of the estimate (SEE) ranged from 260 to 272 kcal·d -1 across equations. Coefficients of determination (R 2 ) ranged from 37% to 42%. The new body mass and FFM-based equations exhibited good agreement based on the constant error (26 and -13 kcal·d -1 ), RMSE (274 and 252 kcal·d -1 ), respectively. CONCLUSIONS: The newly developed equations demonstrated mean bias <2% of measured RMR.

articles.title: Resistance Exercise at Different Periods Before and After Ovariectomy Attenuates Bone Loss in Ovariectomized Mice.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.authors: Yang Xu, Yuting He, Linzhen Rao et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Postmenopausal osteoporosis is a prevalent metabolic bone disease characterized by reduced bone density, decreased bone strength, and increased fracture risk. While resistance exercise has been shown to attenuate osteoporosis, the optimal timing for exercise intervention remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate whether the timing of resistance exercise-initiated before, after, or throughout the period of estrogen deficiency-differentially affects bone health in ovariectomized mice, and to provide a theoretical basis for postmenopausal osteoporosis prevention and treatment with exercise. METHODS: Five-week-old female C57BL/6 mice were assigned to one of five groups: sham operation group (SHAM), ovariectomized sedentary group (OVX), pre-OVX +exercise group (Pre-OVX+E), OVX +exercise group (OVX+E), and post-OVX + exercise group (Post-OVX+E). Mice performed a ladder-climbing resistance exercise protocol at the designated time points. Bone microstructure was assessed by micro-computed tomography, bone biomechanical properties by three-point bending test, osteogenic and osteoclast-related factors by reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction, western blot assays and Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay analysis, and potential regulatory molecular mechanisms through RNA-Seq analysis. RESULTS: All three exercise groups could enhance the bone biomechanical properties and improve the bone microstructure of ovariectomized mice. The Post-OVX+E group performed better than the other exercise groups on microstructure in both cortical bone and cancellous bone. The Post-OVX+E group and the OVX+E group showed better effects on the expression of osteogenic and osteoclast-related factors. RNA-Seq analysis revealed that the extracellular matrix-receptor interaction pathway represented the common signaling pathway shared among groups. CONCLUSIONS: Resistance exercise at different periods before and after ovariectomy can attenuate bone loss in ovariectomized mice, with exercise after ovariectomy demonstrating superior protective benefits on bone. The mechanism underlying these beneficial effects may involve the extracellular matrix-receptor interaction pathway.

articles.title: Superimposed Tendon Vibration Increases Time to Task Failure During Intermittent Isometric Knee Extensions: Effects of Contraction Intensity and Sex.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.authors: Tom Timbert, Nicolas Amiez, Alain Martin et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To determine whether superimposed local vibration (SLV) increases time to task failure (TTF) during submaximal isometric knee extensor contractions at low and moderate intensities (respectively, 30% and 50% of maximal voluntary isometric contraction, MVIC) and to examine whether the SLV effect differs between sexes. METHODS: Fifty-two healthy young adults were assigned to either a 30% or 50% MVIC group ( n = 26 each, 11 women per group). Each group performed a unilateral intermittent isometric knee-extension fatiguing task (15 s contraction/5 s rest) under two randomized conditions (SLV and control, CON), until task failure. Torque and electromyographic (EMG) activity of the knee extensor and flexor muscles were recorded for the entire duration of the task. TTF was defined as the time until torque output dropped more than 10% below the target force. Torque time integral (TTI) was calculated over the TTF. RESULTS: TTF was significantly greater (+9.5 ± 17.3%) in the SLV condition compared with the control ( P < 0.001), independently of contraction intensity (30% vs 50% MVIC, P = 0.901) and sex ( P = 0.183). TTI was greater in SLV than CON (+8.9 ± 17.4%, P < 0.001) with no significant sex or intensity interactions (both P > 0.183). Despite the longer TTF and higher TTI, no difference in EMG during the fatiguing task was observed between conditions ( P > 0.173). CONCLUSIONS: SLV enhances time to failure and force production during submaximal intermittent isometric contractions, regardless of sex or intensity. Unchanged EMG between conditions throughout the fatiguing task suggests greater time spent at high EMG levels with SLV, warranting further investigation.

articles.title: The Effects of Intermittent Hypoxic Training Strategies on Maximal Oxygen Uptake in Healthy Humans: A Meta-analysis with Meta-regression.
articles.authors: Dario Kohlbrenner, Abdallah Ghaith, Joey Fournier et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Intermittent hypoxic training aims to enhance exercise performance and health, commonly assessed through maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max). Currently applied methods are live-high train-low (LHTL), live-low train-high (LLTH) and passive hypoxic conditioning (PHC). However, within these methods, numerous modes of application exist, and effectiveness is debated. OBJECTIVE: To determine the effect of LHTL, LLTH and PHC on VO2max in healthy participants, and identify factors associated with the amplitude of change in VO2max. METHODS: We conducted a systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis and meta-regression. Studies were identified through PubMed, EMBASE and Web of Science. We included controlled studies, calculating between-group standardised mean differences. Athlete and non-athlete populations were analysed separately. RoB2 was used to assess study quality and publication bias was investigated with funnel plots and the Egger's test. RESULTS: Of the 5244 identified studies, 62 were included for analysis, resulting in a sample size of 1332 participants (610 athletes, 722 non-athletes). LHTL increased VO2max significantly more than control in athletes (mean difference [MD] = 2.17; 95% CI = 0.77, 3.56) but not in non-athletes (MD = 3.1; 95% CI = - 0.23, 6.43). LLTH did not increase VO2max significantly more than control in athletes (MD = 0.89; 95% CI = - 0.27, 2.05) but it did in non-athletes (MD = 1.70; 95% CI = 0.85, 2.54). PHC did not increase VO2max significantly more than control in athletes (MD = - 1.07; 95% CI = - 3.51, 1.37) but it did in non-athletes (MD = 2.26; 95% CI = 1.00, 3.52). Multivariate meta-regressions identified the severity, duration, and frequency of hypoxic exposure to be significantly associated with the change in VO2max. CONCLUSIONS: LHTL showed a significant effect on VO2max in athletic populations while LLTH and PHC showed a significant effect on VO2max in non-athletic populations only. Future studies should target investigating which characteristics (e.g. severity, duration) of the hypoxic exposure are most beneficial.

articles.title: Vitamin B6 in Elite Athletes: Potential Implications of High Intakes.
articles.authors: Thomas Valente van Keulen, Nathan A Lewis, Charles R Pedlar
articles.abstract: Vitamin B6 plays a role in over 100 enzymatic reactions, and it is purported that athletes have higher requirements compared with the general population. Deficiency, while rare, may lead to adverse symptoms if severe or prolonged. Conversely, excessive intake may increase the risk of toxicity. This article discusses the potential implications of high vitamin B6 exposure in athletes and includes illustrative observational data on plasma pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP) from routine biomarker monitoring in elite athletes. Observation-level deficiencies (< 30 nmol/L; 5.2%) and raised (> 125 nmol/L; 38.7%) PLP measurements (n = 654) in elite athletes (N = 396) participating in routine biomarker screening, alongside implications of possible intakes above athletes' requirements are discussed. Athletes' use of nutritional supplements, sports beverages, or even intravenous nutrition, which contain highly bioavailable doses of vitamin B6, are a plausible contributor to the observed high PLP concentrations. Chronic total vitamin B6 intake above 21 mg/day, particularly with low protein intake, may increase toxicity risk.

articles.title: Comparison of the Linear versus Non-Linear Repeated Sprint Training on Lower Limb Sports Performance Tasks in Team Sport Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.authors: Seyyed Hadi Asghari, Alexei Wong, Paul Comfort et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Linear repeated sprinf training (LRST) and non-linear repeated sprint training (NLRST) are commonly used to improve sport-specific performance in team-sport athletes; however, their comparative effects on key performance outcomes remain unclear. OBJECTIVE: This systematic review and meta-analysis compared the effects of linear (LRST) and non-linear (NLRST) repeated sprint training on short sprint time (SST), change of direction (COD), aerobic performance indices (API), repeated sprint ability (RSA) performance outcomes and counter movement jump (CMJ) in team sports athletes. METHODS: A comprehensive literature search was conducted in PubMed/Medline, Web of Science, Scopus, Google Scholar, and Embase from inception to 31 July 2025. Eligible studies were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) including competitive team-sport athletes that directly compared LRST and NLRST interventions with a minimum duration of 2 weeks and reported SST as the primary outcome. Secondary outcomes included COD, API, RSA performance, and CMJ. A total of 13 studies (N = 253 athletes) met the inclusion criteria. Standardized mean differences changes (SMDC) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated, with statistical significance set at p ≤ 0.05. Risk of bias and publication bias were assessed using Egger's test, the trim-and-fill method, and funnel plot inspection. RESULTS: Compared with LRST, NLRST showed a favorable effect on the primary outcome (SST) (SMDC = 0.479; 95% CI: - 0.077 to 1.034), with larger effects observed in male athletes, high-volume protocols, and interventions lasting ≥ 12 sessions. For secondary outcomes, NLRST also demonstrated a favorable effect on COD performance (SMDC = 0.601; 95% CI: - 0.131 to 1.332), with a consistent moderate effect size (ES) across subgroups. A greater pooled effect of NLRST was further observed for RSAP outcomes (SMDC = 1.210; 95% CI: 0.559 to 1.861), while API showed a small-to-moderate pooled effect in favor of NLRST (SMDC = - 0.492; 95% CI: - 1.206 to 0.221). In contrast, LRST demonstrated a small-to-moderate pooled advantage for CMJ performance (SMDC = 0.418; 95% CI: - 0.236 to 1.072), with larger effects evident in male athletes, elite players, and high-volume or longer-duration programs, with high‑volume protocols demonstrating a large and statistically significant effect. CONCLUSION: Overall, NLRST appears to be more favorable than LRST for improving SST, COD, APIs, and RSAP performance outcomes, particularly in trained athletes and high-volume training contexts, whereas LRST shows a greater benefit for CMJ performance, especially in longer-duration and higher-volume programs. These findings suggest that the selection of sprint training structure should be aligned with the specific performance qualities targeted and the sport-specific physiological demands. However, the interpretation of these results should consider several limitations, including heterogeneity in outcome measures and training protocols, the predominance of soccer-based and male samples, limited reporting of external load monitoring, and variability in aerobic and repeated-sprint assessment methods, which may affect generalizability and mechanistic interpretation.

articles.title: Beyond imbalance: an elasticity framework for the distance-averaged force-velocity relationship in vertical jump.
articles.authors: Zhaoqian Li, Mingyu Li, Xing Zhang et al.
articles.abstract: This study aimed to (1) establish the distance‑averaged F‑V relationship framework and (2) develop elasticity metrics that quantify how F‑V relationship variables govern jump height and inform training decisions. Theoretical derivation and experimental validation across 108 F-V relationship models derived from 1578 jumps (countermovement jump and squat jump at three knee angles; 20 well-trained subjects) yielded a systematic error of - 2.1% and a strong linear association (r = 0.96, 95% CI [0.93; 0.97]) between measured and predicted jump height. Four elasticity metrics were formulated: force elasticity ([Formula: see text]), the elasticity of jump height to maximal force ([Formula: see text]); velocity elasticity ([Formula: see text]), the elasticity of jump height to maximal velocity ([Formula: see text]); the force-velocity elasticity norm [Formula: see text], reflecting the overall sensitivity of jump height to changes in F-V relationship variables; and the force-velocity elasticity ratio [Formula: see text]), indicating which variable dominates the jump height response. Simulations and experiments revealed that [Formula: see text] bore an inverse relationship to [Formula: see text], and [Formula: see text] was inversely related to [Formula: see text], reflecting diminishing marginal returns. At a fixed jump height, simulations showed [Formula: see text] and [Formula: see text] displayed a U-shaped relationship; a balanced profile ([Formula: see text] = 1) did not always correspond to the lowest [Formula: see text]. The distance-averaged F-V elasticity framework offers a physically grounded and quantitative tool for linking F-V relationship variables directly to jump performance, providing a basis for informing individualized training decisions.

articles.title: Visual external focus of attention modulates corticospinal excitation-inhibition balance after acute exercise.
articles.authors: Philipp Bauer, João H Oliveira, João S Gomes et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Individuals are frequently instructed to adopt an internal focus during exercise, such as concentrating on a specific muscle, which may inadvertently lead to online conscious motor processing and constrain automatic motor control. In contrast, an external focus, particularly with distant visual feedback, is thought to benefit corticospinal modulation, enhancing automaticity and movement complexity. Nonetheless, the effective integration of attentional focus into evidence-based exercise prescription requires a mechanistic understanding of its neurophysiological basis. Therefore, this study investigated whether a single exercise bout performed with visual external, external or internal focus differentially modulates corticospinal excitation-inhibition balance (Corticospinal Excitability/Silent Period ratio), short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI), intracortical facilitation (ICF) and torque complexity. METHODS: Thirty-seven healthy young adults were randomised to internal (12), external (12), or visual external focus (13) groups, completing a seated calf-raise bout to failure under the respective focus of attention instruction. Neurophysiological outcomes were assessed using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and analysed in a linear mixed-effects model. RESULTS: Corticospinal excitation-inhibition balance was enhanced after an exercise bout carried out with a visual external focus (increase 1.40 ± 0.42 mV/s, p = 0.005), while no changes were detected with an external or internal focus (all p ≥ 0.05). SICI, ICF and torque complexity showed no significant effect regarding attentional focus. CONCLUSION: The present study contributes to the neurophysiological basis for using goal-oriented visual feedback cues to increase corticospinal drive, offering a targeted intervention strategy which has potential to optimize motor performance in elite athletes and accelerate functional recovery in clinical populations. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: The present study was registered under NCT06538766 on 26/07/2024.

articles.title: New decompression gas CF₄/O₂: reducing DCS risk and ameliorating injuries in male rats.
articles.authors: Jiaqi Li, Hong Chen, Zhi Li et al.
articles.abstract: Decompression sickness (DCS) remains a major risk in diving. Prolonging decompression reduces inert gas load but increases operation time and underwater exposure. We tested a carbon tetrafluoride-oxygen mixture (CF₄/O₂) as a decompression gas in two rat decompression protocols: 6 ATA compressed air and 9 ATA helium-oxygen (heliox). Switching to CF₄/O₂ 10 min before decompression significantly reduced DCS incidence in both protocols: air, 68% (19/28) to 11% (3/28); heliox, 68% (15/22) to 18% (4/22). Mortality was significantly reduced in the compressed-air protocol (29% [8/28] to 0 [0/28], P = 0.004) but not in the heliox protocol (14% [3/22] to 0 [0/22], P = 0.233). Echocardiography showed fewer or no intracardiac bubbles after CF₄/O₂. In the heliox protocol, CF₄/O₂ significantly modulated some pulmonary function parameters; in the compressed-air protocol, pulmonary function changes were time-dependent and did not differ significantly between groups. CF₄/O₂ also reduced lung inflammation, endothelial injury, and histological damage in both protocols. In a 28-day repeated hyperbaric exposure protocol assessing selected serum biochemical endpoints, CF₄/O₂ did not increase serum alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, creatinine or urea; however, this protocol did not include post-exposure histopathology or haematology, so safety conclusions are limited to the measured endpoints. These findings support the tested CF₄/O₂ gas-switching strategy under the specific conditions used. Shorter decompression protocols were not tested, and shortening decompression time remains a potential application rather than a demonstrated outcome.

articles.title: Neuromechanical associations in vertical jump adaptation after plyometric training: a multivariate meta-analysis.
articles.authors: Lin Xie, Jing Dai, BingHong Gao et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Plyometric training (PT) is widely used to enhance vertical-jump performance, but the associations between muscle-tendon mechanical adaptation, lower-limb sEMG amplitude, and" performance across jump tasks with different neuromechanical demands remain incompletely understood. In particular, whether stiffness adaptations are uniformly beneficial across Stretch-Shortening Cycle(SSC)-dependent and predominantly concentric jump tasks remains unclear. OBJECTIVE: This study employed a multivariate meta-analysis to quantify associations between changes in vertical stiffness (Kvert), Achilles tendon stiffness (Ktendon), knee-extensor and plantar-flexor sEMG amplitude, and vertical-jump adaptation, while examining whether these associations differed according to jump type and intervention duration. METHODS: In strict accordance with PRISMA guidelines, seven major databases were searched for randomized controlled trials from inception to December 2025. Multivariate random-effects models were constructed using the metaSEM package in R, supplemented by Pearson correlation analysis. The GRADE framework was utilized to assess the certainty of evidence. RESULTS: Twenty-nine randomized controlled trials were included. Plyometric training significantly improved vertical jump outcomes (all p < 0.05; standardized mean differences(SMD) > 0.40), vertical stiffness (SMD = 0.37; 95% CI, 0.07-0.67), and Achilles tendon stiffness (SMD = 0.43). Descriptive Kvert-VJ correlations were positive for CMJ (r = 0.51) and negative for DJ (r = - 0.72). Formal moderator analysis supported differences in the Kvert-VJ association across jump types (LRT = 11.33, df = 2, p = 0.003) but not across intervention-duration categories (LRT = 2.05, df = 2, p = 0.358). Formal moderation by jump type or intervention duration was not observed for Ktendon or the sEMG outcomes, although these analyses were based on relatively few studies. CONCLUSION: Plyometric-training adaptations showed formal evidence of task-specific Kvert-VJ associations, whereas duration-specific moderation was not supported. Associations involving Ktendon and sEMG amplitude were less consistent and should be regarded as exploratory.

articles.title: Aerobic exercise preconditioning enhances skeletal muscle resistance and recovery after contusion: involvement of the SIRT1/PGC-1α axis.
articles.authors: Wei Wang, Zhao Tian, Peijin Li et al.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Compared with passive recovery after injury, exercise preconditioning may provide an active strategy for improving the subsequent response of skeletal muscle to injury. This study aimed to investigate the effects of aerobic exercise preconditioning (AEP) on skeletal muscle injury (SMI) and post-injury repair, with particular focus on the involvement of the SIRT1/PGC-1α axis and changes in PGC-1α acetylation. METHODS: This study initially investigated the effects of continuous aerobic exercise on skeletal muscle in healthy mice. Subsequently, the influence of AEP on injury severity and regenerative repair of the gastrocnemius muscle was examined in mice with SMI. Western blotting was used to determine the expression levels of SIRT1 and PGC-1α proteins, immunoprecipitation was performed to assess the acetylation status of PGC-1α, and qRT-PCR was used to analyze the expression of genes associated with mitochondrial biogenesis-related markers and muscle regeneration. Finally, the involvement of SIRT1 signaling in the AEP-associated response to SMI was further examined using the pharmacological SIRT1 inhibitor EX527. RESULTS: Continuous aerobic exercise was associated with increased SIRT1/PGC-1α signaling and changes in mitochondrial biogenesis-related markers in the gastrocnemius muscle of healthy mice. AEP was associated with reduced injury-related changes and an improved post-injury repair profile in mice with SMI. During the early stage after injury, AEP was accompanied by sustained SIRT1/ PGC-1α signaling and reduced PGC-1α acetylation. Pharmacological inhibition of SIRT1 with EX527 partially attenuated the AEP-associated protective and reparative effects on the injured gastrocnemius muscle. CONCLUSION: These findings suggest that AEP establishes an adaptive state in skeletal muscle that is associated with reduced injury-related damage and an enhanced post-injury reparative response. The SIRT1/PGC-1α axis and altered PGC-1α acetylation may contribute to these AEP-associated effects.

articles.title: Neural, contractile, and muscular determinants associated with lower strength in recreationally active older men: a cross-sectional study.
articles.authors: Ronan Sherman, Mathias Forsberg Brobakken, Ole Kristian Berg et al.
articles.abstract: Skeletal muscle strength declines with age. However, the relative contributions of various neuromuscular factors to this decline appear to not be fully understood. Thus, we compared relative attenuations in key neural and muscular strength determinants with age, in vivo and in vitro, recruiting 22 old (75 ± 1 years) and 18 young (25 ± 1 years) recreationally active men. Leg extension maximal voluntary contraction (MVC), early (0-100 ms) and late (0-200 ms) rate of force development (RFD), were reduced by - 39%, - 55%, and - 49%, respectively, in the old (all p < 0.001); however, estimated thigh cross-sectional area (CSA) was not different between groups. In contrast, efferent neural drive assessed by evoked recordings (m.soleus normalized V-waves; V/Msup), largely dependent on corticospinal factors, revealed a - 72% age-related reduction (p < 0.001). A - 51% reduction was also observed in peripheral motoneuron excitability, measured as Hmax/Mmax at 10% MVC (p < 0.001). The neural age-related decline was confirmed applying peak electromyography (EMG; - 14%), early (- 31%), and late (- 30%; all p < 0.05) rate of EMG rise, during leg extension MVC. While voluntary activation was unaltered with age, quadriceps contractility was reduced (resting twitch: peak force, - 41%; RFD, - 43%; delay, +39%; time-to-relaxation, +56%; all p < 0.01). Biopsies from m.vastus lateralis showed an age-related decrease in proportion, - 16% (type II: 43% (old) vs. 51% (young); p < 0.001), but not size, of fast twitch fibers. Concomitantly, slow twitch fibers were 12% larger in old vs. young (p < 0.05). Collectively, these findings showed that age-related reductions in muscle strength were accompanied by pronounced alterations in neural function alongside changes in muscle phenotype, despite preserved thigh CSA.

articles.title: Longitudinal transcriptomic monitoring of erythropoietic adaptations in endurance athletes: a prospective study protocol.
articles.authors: Sushmita Kumari, T K Sanjith, Jayaseelan Murgaiyan et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Understanding systemic molecular adaptations to endurance training and environmental hypoxia is important for advancing physiological monitoring in athletes. Transcriptomic profiling of peripheral blood mononuclear cells offers a promising approach to characterising erythropoiesis-related biological responses, yet longitudinal data under real-world training conditions remain limited. This protocol describes the rationale and design of a prospective longitudinal study aimed at investigating erythropoiesis-related transcriptomic adaptations to variations in training load and hypoxic exposure in endurance athletes. METHODS: A total of 60 trained endurance athletes will be followed over a 12-month period, encompassing baseline conditioning, intensified training phases, competition, recovery, and altitude exposure, where applicable. Training load will be quantified using daily session logs and wearable-derived metrics. Peripheral blood samples will be collected at baseline and monthly intervals, with additional sampling during key physiological phases. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells will undergo transcriptomic profiling using high-throughput gene-expression platforms, with pathway-focused analysis targeting hypoxia signalling, erythroid differentiation, iron metabolism, and angiogenic regulation. Longitudinal statistical modelling will be employed to evaluate adaptation trajectories, intra-individual variability, and associations between transcriptomic responses and quantified training exposures. EXPECTED RESULTS: The study is expected to identify phase-dependent modulation of erythropoiesis-related transcriptional pathways and to enable estimation of physiological ranges of molecular variability across training cycles. Repeated within-individual assessment may provide insight into the persistence and magnitude of transcriptional responses to training stress and hypoxic stimuli. CONCLUSION: This longitudinal framework is anticipated to generate foundational evidence supporting the feasibility of transcriptomic monitoring in athletic populations and to inform future development of advanced biological surveillance strategies in sport.

articles.title: Adipocyte lipolysis is a determinant of skeletal muscle size during fasting and feeding.
articles.journal: American journal of physiology. Endocrinology and metabolism
articles.authors: Daniel M Marko, Rhea V Vemula, Meghan O Conn et al.
articles.abstract: Intermittent fasting (IF) can lower fat mass, but also muscle mass. The mechanisms governing tissue partitioning during fasting remain unclear. During fasting, adipose-derived fatty acids from lipolysis and lipolysis-fueled hepatic ketogenesis maintain blood glucose and systemic energy homeostasis. We hypothesized that impaired lipolysis during fasting would shift substrate provision from adipose to muscle, increasing muscle catabolism during IF. We tested male adipocyte-specific adipose triglyceride lipase knockout (aKO) and littermate floxed-control mice during ad libitum feeding on a 10-wk 5:2 IF protocol consisting of two nonconsecutive 24-h fasts and 5 ad libitum feeding days per week. After 10 wk of IF, aKO mice had lower blood lipids and ketones and lost more lean mass and less fat mass than floxed-control mice when mice were fed a standard control diet and also retained more inguinal white adipose tissue and had lower hindlimb muscle mass when IF was compared with ad libitum feeding. In addition, aKO mice had larger adipocytes, smaller muscle fibers, and increased expression of the atrogene, Atrogin1. We then provided exogenous lipids by feeding an obesogenic high-fat diet (HFD). HFD-fed aKO mice had higher whole body fat oxidation and lower blood lipids and ketones than floxed-controls. Obese HFD-fed aKO mice still had smaller skeletal muscle myofibers and increased muscle atrogene expression despite smaller adipocytes during ad libitum feeding or IF. Therefore, adipocyte ATGL-mediated lipolysis is a determinant of skeletal muscle size, and lower lipolysis influences the balance of fat vs. muscle loss during fasting.NEW & NOTEWORTHY This study demonstrates that adipocyte ATGL is a critical regulator of adipose-muscle metabolic crosstalk. Limiting adipocyte lipolysis through adipose ATGL deletion reduced blood lipid and ketone fuel availability, thereby increasing adipose retention, decreasing skeletal muscle mass and fiber size, and increasing muscle atrogene expression, particularly during intermittent fasting. These findings support a model in which impaired adipocyte lipid mobilization shifts whole body energy demands away from adipose and toward skeletal muscle, promoting muscle catabolism during fasting.

articles.title: The relationship between eosinophil and macrophage abundance in human visceral adipose tissue in healthy individuals.
articles.journal: American journal of physiology. Endocrinology and metabolism
articles.authors: Karel Paukner, Barbora Muffova, Hana Bartuskova et al.
articles.abstract: Animal studies have linked adipose tissue eosinophils to metabolic homeostasis through IL-4-dependent mechanisms; however, corresponding data from human visceral adipose tissue (VAT), particularly in healthy individuals, remain limited. We analyzed eosinophil abundance (CD45+CD14-CD16-CD15+) in visceral adipose tissue (VAT) obtained from 47 apparently healthy living kidney donors (31 women and 16 men). The eosinophil association with anti-inflammatory CD14+CD16- and proinflammatory CD14+CD16+ macrophages and eosinophil distribution across perivascular adipose tissue (PVAT) and blood were investigated. Eosinophil percentage in VAT was positively correlated with the proportion of anti-inflammatory CD14+CD16- macrophages (r = 0.40, 95% CI 0.19-0.61, P = 0.005). Eosinophil abundance in VAT was positively correlated with eosinophil levels in both PVAT and blood, with a stronger association observed between visceral and perivascular depots. In a multivariable linear regression model, the previously reported association between non-HDL cholesterol and the proportion of anti-inflammatory macrophages was confirmed, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein was identified as an additional negative predictor. In the multivariable model, VAT eosinophil percentage was not independently associated with anti-inflammatory macrophage proportion (P = 0.109). Plasma IL-4 concentrations remained within a narrow range across all participants. These findings extend the limited evidence on eosinophils in human VAT and underscore the need to define their specific functions within the adipose tissue immune network, including whether and how they contribute to macrophage polarization and immunometabolic homeostasis.NEW & NOTEWORTHY This study provides quantitative data on eosinophil abundance in human visceral adipose tissue from apparently healthy individuals, a tissue that is rarely available for research. A positive association between eosinophils and anti-inflammatory CD14+CD16- macrophages was identified, representing, to our knowledge, the first quantitative evidence of this relationship in human visceral adipose tissue, which is closely linked to metabolic health.

articles.title: Exercise-mimicking effect of exogenous lactate administration: promoting visceral fat reduction via ventromedial hypothalamic SF-1 neurons in female rats.
articles.journal: American journal of physiology. Endocrinology and metabolism
articles.authors: Jinchan Du, Zhaomin Zhang, Jing Han et al.
articles.abstract: Lactate, a metabolic product of high-intensity training, may possess exercise-mimicking effects that promote fat loss via the hypothalamic-adipose axis, yet its neuronal targets remain unclear. This study investigated whether lactate administration mimics high-intensity training (HIT)-induced fat loss through steroidogenic factor-1 (SF-1) neurons in the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH). Female SD rats fed a high-fat diet were subjected to a 6-wk intervention. The results showed that chronic lactate administration independently reduced visceral adipose tissue (VAT) mass and enhanced the resting fat oxidation rate more effectively than moderate-intensity aerobic training, which conversely suppressed postexercise lipolysis. The VAT loss was accompanied by neuroplastic changes in the VMH and upregulated markers of sympathetic capacity in adipose tissue. In contrast, chemogenetic inhibition of VMH SF-1 neurons using designer receptors exclusively activated by designer drugs reversed the lactate-mediated electrophysiological changes and abolished the elevation in resting metabolic rate, confirming the necessity of this neuronal population for the metabolic effects of lactate. These findings demonstrate that lactate acts as a central exerkine, activating VMH SF-1 neurons, which correlates with an upregulated capacity for sympathetic nervous system-mediated VAT reduction, thereby providing a mechanistic explanation for the superior efficacy of HIT in managing central obesity.NEW & NOTEWORTHY This study identifies lactate as a key central signal that mimics the VAT-reducing effects of HIT. We demonstrate that lactate administration activates SF-1 neurons in the VMH, triggering a sympathetic drive that promotes lipolysis in female rats. Crucially, chemogenetic inhibition of these neurons abolishes lactate's metabolic benefits, establishing a direct causal link between lactate signaling and the central regulation of adipose tissue.
