articles.title: Graft integration in autologous costal cartilage transplantation: a long-term study using chondrocyte-laden fibrin gel.
articles.authors: A D Kurenkova, S A Sheleg, Y M Efremov et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Mosaicplasty of articular cartilage can be performed using costal cartilage due to its structural similarity. This method has been successfully applied in clinical practice for small joints; however, its use in large joints is limited, partly due to graft displacement. In this study, we used chondrocyte-laden fibrin gel to improve integration in a rat model of autologous costal cartilage transplantation into a knee joint defect and assessed long-term outcomes. METHODS: Costal cartilage was characterized histologically, immunohistochemically, and biomechanically. Autologous grafts were harvested from the tenth rib and implanted into knee defects pretreated with chondrocyte-laden fibrin gel. Controls included cell-free fibrin gel, defect-only control, and sham-operated animals. Graft integration, subchondral bone resorption, and graft composition were analyzed at 1, 6, and 12 months using micro-CT, histology, and immunostaining. RESULTS: Costal cartilage demonstrated histological and biomechanical properties comparable to articular cartilage. Chondrocyte-laden fibrin gel did not significantly improve integration but reduced subchondral bone resorption, a preliminary finding consistent with an anti-inflammatory effect. Retained grafts restored joint congruity, integrated with host tissue, and showed no resorption or loss of hyaline cartilage markers over 12 months, despite age-related osteoarthritis changes in surrounding tissue. CONCLUSIONS: Although chondrocyte-laden fibrin gel did not enhance graft integration, this study demonstrates long-term structural preservation of costal cartilage grafts in a rat knee defect model. Further studies in larger animals are needed to optimize integration strategies and support translation into clinical practice, potentially expanding treatment options for patients with limited donor tissue.

articles.title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence or Telerehabilitation on Consumer Ratings in Physical Therapy: An Online Randomized Experiment.
articles.authors: Megan H Ross, Joshua Simmich, Daniela Berg et al.
articles.abstract: IMPORTANCE: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into health care delivery, but its influence on consumer perceptions of physical therapist services remains unclear. OBJECTIVE: The objective was to examine how the use of AI influences consumer perceptions of in-person and telerehabilitation physical therapist services. DESIGN: This study used a randomized 2 × 2 factorial experimental design comparing AI use and delivery mode. SETTING: The experiment was conducted online in Australia. PARTICIPANTS: The study included 710 Australian adults recruited through a paid panel. EXPOSURE: Participants were randomized to 1 of 4 hypothetical physical therapist consultation scenarios (in-person vs telerehabilitation; AI used vs not used). MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Perceived warmth; competence; safety; provider trust; emotional trust; relational and functional service quality; working alliance; and intention to use were measured on 7-point Likert-scales. Composite mean scores were analyzed using ordinary least squares regression with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors. RESULTS: Mean scores in the no-AI, in-person condition ranged from 4.8 to 5.8. Among in-person scenarios, described AI use was associated with lower ratings across all outcomes, including warmth (b = -0.3, 95% CI = -0.5 to -0.1), competence (-0.4, -0.6 to -0.2) and safety (-0.8, -1.1 to -0.6), provider trust (-0.5, -0.7 to -0.3) and intention to use (-0.8, -1.0 to -0.5). Without AI, telerehabilitation also reduced ratings by 0.2 to 0.7 points across outcomes. Positive interaction effects indicated attenuation of AI-related reductions in telerehabilitation for relational (interaction b = 0.4, 95% CI = 0.1 to 0.8) and functional service quality (0.36, 0.02 to 0.70), intention to use (0.6, 0.1 to 1.0), and perceived safety (0.5, 0.1 to 0.9). CONCLUSIONS: Hypothetical in-person consultations described as involving AI were associated with poorer consumer perceptions of physical therapists and services. Telerehabilitation was also perceived less favorably than in-person care. RELEVANCE: Future studies should test whether transparency and reassurance mitigate the effects of AI-use on consumer perceptions of physical therapy.

articles.title: Antenatal multiple micronutrients versus iron-folic acid supplementation and infant neurodevelopment: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
articles.authors: Jitender Nagpal, Sarika Tyagi, Swapnil Rawat et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Antenatal multiple micronutrient (MMN) supplementation reduces the risk of low birth weight and small-for-gestational-age birth compared with iron and folic acid (IFA), but whether the benefits extend to neurodevelopment remains uncertain. OBJECTIVES: To estimate the effect of antenatal MMN compared with IFA on infant cognitive, motor, and language development up to 24 months of age. METHODS: We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, the Cochrane Library, Google Scholar, OpenGrey, Wiley Online Library, and trial registers through June 10, 2026 for randomized controlled trials comparing antenatal MMN with IFA and reporting infant neurodevelopment. Two reviewers independently screened and extracted data; risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2 and certainty with GRADE. Hedges g estimates were pooled with a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model and Knapp-Hartung adjustment; cluster-trial variances were inflated by the design effect. RESULTS: Of 2,943 records, seven trials (8 reports; 5,331 infants for the cognitive comparison) were included. MMN and IFA did not differ in cognitive development (g = +0.02; 95% CI -0.06, +0.10; P = 0.53; I2 = 13%) or motor development (g = -0.02; 95% CI -0.09, +0.05; P = 0.49; I2 = 0%). Language showed a small, non-significant advantage for MMN that was not robust across sensitivity analyses (g = +0.07; 95% CI -0.00, +0.14; P = 0.06; I2 = 0%). All pooled point estimates were below the conventional threshold for a small, standardized effect of 0.2. Certainty was moderate for cognitive and motor outcomes and low for language. CONCLUSIONS: Antenatal MMN supplementation was associated with little to no difference in infant cognitive or motor development compared with IFA up to 24 months of age. The small language difference was not statistically significant, was not robust across sensitivity analyses, and is unlikely to be clinically important. PROTOCOL AND REGISTRATION: PROSPERO CRD420261392389. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261392389.

articles.title: Dietary threonine requirement of healthy older adults >60y stratified by age and sex in a repeated measures design1.
articles.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
articles.authors: Alyssa Paoletti, Wala Naeem, Paul B Pencharz et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Current dietary guidelines for most of the world recommend increased plant protein consumption to improve health and support environmental sustainability. Threonine is an indispensable AA required for protein and mucin synthesis which is present in low concentrations in plant proteins. Threonine requirement is needed to guide dietary planning and assessment of protein adequacy particularly in those consuming predominantly plant-based protein diets. However, no data exist on dietary threonine requirement in older adults. OBJECTIVES: 1) Determine the threonine requirement in older adults using the indicator amino acid oxidation (IAAO) method in a repeated measures design. 2) compare the derived estimates based on age: 60-69y and 70-79y and sex. METHODS: The threonine requirement was determined using the IAAO method with L-[1-13C] phenylalanine as the indicator. Twenty-two older adults >60 y (n = 10 males and n = 12 females) were randomly assigned to receive up to 7 threonine intakes (5 to 35 mg/kg/d). The mean threonine requirement was determined from oxidation of L-[1-13C] phenylalanine (F13CO2) using a two-phase linear mixed effect model. The 95% CI was calculated using parametric bootstrap. The overlap of the 95% CI between the 2 age groups were used to compare the requirement estimates. The null hypothesis was accepted if the interval contained zero. RESULTS: There was no effect of sex on the threonine requirement. However, the threonine requirement for adults 60-69y and 70-79y were 11 mg/kg/d (R2m = 0.10, R2c = 0.81; 7.70, 14.30 mg/kg/d) and 17.9 mg/kg/d (R2m = 0.44, R2c = 0.64; 13.23, 22.57 mg/kg/d) respectively with those 70-79y having a higher requirement than those 60-69y ( -1.18, -12.62). CONCLUSIONS: The result of the current study demonstrates that AA needs among older adults change within decades of age. This should be integrated into future AA recommendations for accurate planning and assessment of protein nutrition in the elderly. The trial was registered at Clinical Trials Registry: # NCT02008955, https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06225648.

articles.title: Temporal Eating Patterns Show Inconsistent Associations With Cancer Incidence and Mortality: Systematic Review of Prospective Studies.
articles.authors: Sihan Song, Tuo Lan, Seho Park et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Temporal eating patterns, such as eating time, frequency, and regularity, may be associated with cancer outcomes through circadian and metabolic pathways, but evidence remains limited. OBJECTIVES: We aimed to systematically review prospective studies examining associations between temporal eating patterns and cancer incidence or mortality. METHODS: Following PRISMA guidelines, PubMed and Embase were searched from inception to September 2, 2026. Eligible studies included prospective cohorts of adults assessing eating or fasting duration, nighttime eating, breakfast frequency or timing, meal regularity, or eating frequency in relation to cancer incidence or mortality. Meta-analyses were conducted when ≥3 studies examined comparable exposure-outcome pairs, and the quality of meta-evidence was evaluated using the NutriGrade scoring system. Risk of bias was assessed using the Risk of Bias for Nutrition Observational Studies tool. RESULTS: Seventeen prospective cohort studies were included. Findings for eating or fasting duration and nighttime eating varied across studies for both cancer incidence and mortality. Lower breakfast frequency was associated with higher cancer mortality and colorectal cancer incidence in some studies, but not with breast cancer incidence. Greater eating-time variability and unrestrained eating were associated with higher cancer mortality, with unrestrained eating also associated with higher colorectal cancer incidence. Associations between eating frequency and cancer outcomes varied across studies and cancer sites. A meta-analysis of three studies showed a non-significant inverse association between eating frequency and colorectal cancer incidence in both categorical (HR = 0.81, 95% CI: 0.64-1.03) and dose-response analyses (HR per 1 time/day increase = 0.95, 95% CI: 0.89-1.01), with very low-quality meta-evidence. Risk of bias varied across domains, with common concerns related to confounding and exposure changes over follow-up. CONCLUSIONS: Findings from cohort studies suggest potential associations between temporal eating patterns and cancer outcomes, but the evidence remains limited and heterogeneous, underscoring the need for further investigation. PROSPERO REGISTRATION: CRD420251246423.

articles.title: UCI Sports Nutrition Project: Position Statement on Nutrition for Cycling.
articles.journal: International journal of sport nutrition and exercise metabolism
articles.authors: Louise M Burke, Eimear Dolan, Javier T Gonzalez et al.
articles.abstract: Nutrition is a key determinant of cycling performance, underpinning the ability to optimize on-bike performance, support training adaptation and recovery, and maintain rider health and well-being. While these goals are shared across disciplines, the diverse physiological demands and logistical constraints of different cycling disciplines present distinct nutritional challenges. In recognition of both the importance of nutrition and the diverse individual and discipline-specific demands of cycling, the Union Cycliste Internationale Sports Nutrition Project was established and led by a steering committee that synthesized the expertise of 54 researchers to identify key nutritional requirements for elite cycling and develop recommendations that account for both individual and discipline-specific needs. These insights were published within a series of 14 topic-specific reviews. In this position statement, we present the principal take-home messages from the overall project, organized into 10 overarching themes spanning performance preparation, in-competition fueling, recovery and adaptation, energy availability, physique management, protecting against illness and injury, technological support, the use of supplements and sports foods, and age- and sex-specific considerations. Cycling-specific considerations are used to develop targeted nutritional recommendations within each of these themes, and high-priority future research directions are identified.

articles.title: Menstrual Cycle Phase Is Associated With Changes in Body Weight, Bioimpedance, and Carbohydrate Intake, but Not in Resting Metabolic Rate in Physically Active Females.
articles.journal: International journal of sport nutrition and exercise metabolism
articles.authors: Michaela Wagner, Adam Wagner, Ida Löfberg et al.
articles.abstract: This observational repeated-measures study investigated the effect of three menstrual cycle phases on resting metabolic rate (RMR), body composition, and dietary intake in 21 naturally menstruating, physically active females (age 24.9 ± 4.1 years; height 168.4 ± 7.8 cm). Measurements were scheduled during the early follicular (EFP), ovulatory, and mid-luteal (MLP) phases using menstrual bleeding onset and urinary luteinizing hormone tests. RMR was measured using indirect calorimetry, body composition via multifrequency bioelectrical impedance analysis, and dietary intake through 3-day food records. Linear mixed-effects models revealed no statistically significant differences in RMR across phases (p = .148). Most dietary intake variables remained stable across the cycle (all p ≥ .074); however, absolute carbohydrate intake was significantly higher in the EFP (234 ± 48 g) than in the MLP (209 ± 53 g; p = .037). Body weight significantly decreased from the EFP (65.2 ± 7.4 kg) to the MLP (64.9 ± 7.3 kg; p = .029). Similarly, the extracellular water ratio decreased (0.376 ± 0.004 vs. 0.374 ± 0.005; p = .019), and phase angle increased (5.85 ± 0.45 vs. 5.98 ± 0.53; p = .021) between the EFP and the MLP. Estimates of fat-free mass and body fat percentage did not differ (p > .05). In physically active females, RMR and most dietary intake variables remained statistically stable across the cycle, whereas carbohydrate intake was higher in EFP than in MLP. Observed fluctuations in body weight and bioimpedance metrics likely reflect hydration shifts rather than changes in tissue composition.

articles.title: Fuel Doesn't Fix It: Oculomotor Control Declines During 3 Hr of Exercise Irrespective of Carbohydrate Availability.
articles.journal: International journal of sport nutrition and exercise metabolism
articles.authors: Charlotte J W Connell, Shelley Duncan, Joanna M Black et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: This study investigates whether carbohydrate supplementation during 3 hr of cycling attenuates postexercise changes in oculomotor control and visual performance. METHODS: Within a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled, repeated-measures, crossover design, nine healthy males completed two 180-min cycling trials at 60% of maximal aerobic capacity, ingesting either a carbohydrate (0.7 g·kg-1·hr-1) or placebo solution. Saccadic eye movements (rapid, ballistic gaze shifts used to redirect the fovea to targets of interest), visual acuity, binocular function, and global motion perception were assessed before and after exercise. Heart rate, perceived exertion, blood glucose, and serum insulin levels were monitored throughout exercise. RESULTS: Blood glucose diverged significantly between conditions across the 180-min exercise protocol, reaching hypoglycemic levels (<4 mmol/L) in placebo from 150 min (placebo: 3.2 ± 0.4 vs. carbohydrate: 5.2 ± 0.7 mmol/L at 180 min). Postexercise saccade velocity, amplitude, and latency changed equivalently across both conditions (-13% velocity, -1° amplitude, +25-ms latency; all p < .01). Visual attention, global motion perception, visual acuity, and binocular function were unchanged by exercise or intervention. CONCLUSION: Postexercise reductions in saccade velocity and amplitude, and increased latency, were observed regardless of glycemic state, reflecting impaired oculomotor output independent of carbohydrate availability, while visual performance was preserved. These findings point toward a centrally mediated neural mechanism rather than carbohydrate substrate limitation.

articles.title: Influence of Guideline-Based Carbohydrate Intake on Training Adaptations, Health, and Sleep in Female Rugby Athletes: An Exploratory Study.
articles.journal: International journal of sport nutrition and exercise metabolism
articles.authors: Rebekka Frazer, Christopher D Askew, Amy-Lee Bowler et al.
articles.abstract: This exploratory study examined the effect of carbohydrate and subsequent energy availability (EA) on training adaptations, health, and sleep metrics across a 7-week preseason in semiprofessional female rugby union athletes. Full food provision on training days (four/week) manipulated carbohydrate intake: 6 versus 3 g·kg-1·day-1 for intervention (n = 7) and CON (n = 6), respectively while standardizing protein intake (>1.2 g·kg-1·day-1). Nontraining days involved ad libitum intake. Quantification of exercise energy expenditure via an individually calibrated wearable device allowed estimation of EA. Strength (three-repetition max squat, bench pull, and bench press), Bronco shuttle time; countermovement jump; biomarkers including iron studies, thyroid function, and cholesterol; sleep metrics; and physique (four-compartment model) were assessed before and after preseason. Training day carbohydrate intake was higher in intervention than CON (6.3 ± 0.2 vs. 3.1 ± 0.2 g·kg-1·day-1, p < .001), resulting in higher EA across the preseason (45.0 ± 5.8 vs. 29.9 ± 5.8 kcal·kg-1 fat-free mass-1·day-1, p < .001). Significant time effects were observed for bench pull (+3.6 kg, p = .024) and bench press (+4.6 kg, p = .011), fat mass (-1.1 kg, p < .001), fat-free mass (+1.2 kg, p = .025), and ferritin (-29 μg/L, p = .009). No significant interaction was observed for training adaptations, physique, or biochemical markers. Greater sleep duration was observed in CON on training nights, F(1, 156.072) = 5.821, p = .017, although other sleep metrics showed limited between-group differences. While increased carbohydrate intake improved EA, it had limited effect on training adaptations, health, or sleep metrics in this small, exploratory cohort.

articles.title: The Effect of a Repetitive Feeding Challenge With Carbohydrate Versus Fat on Markers of Gastrointestinal Integrity and Systemic Outcomes in Response to Endurance Exercise.
articles.journal: International journal of sport nutrition and exercise metabolism
articles.authors: Isabel G Martinez, Jessica R Biesiekierski, Christopher E Rauch et al.
articles.abstract: Athletes report consuming nutritionally dense foods before and during exercise to manage gastrointestinal symptoms (GIS). The study investigated whether fat, compared with carbohydrate (CHO), as a gut-training supplement, compromises gastrointestinal integrity and triggers systemic inflammation in response to endurance exercise. Thirty-six endurance athletes (seven females and 29 males) completed a preintervention gut-challenge trial (T1), involving a 2-hr run (60%V˙O2max) with CHO gel intake every 20 min (87 g/hr), followed by a 1-hr self-paced distance test. Participants were randomized to a fat (FFC; 20 g nut butter) or CHO supplement (CFC; 47 g CHO gel) for a feeding-challenge protocol (1 hr exercise with supplement for 7 days), followed by a gut-challenge retrial (T2). During T1 and T2, blood samples were collected before and after exercise to measure intestinal fatty-acid binding protein (I-FABP), soluble CD14 (sCD14), and C-reactive protein (CRP). Pre- to postexercise peak responses were similar within and between groups for plasma I-FABP (FFC: 254 ± 495 vs. 349 ± 622 pg/ml, p = .911; CFC: 344 ± 336 vs. 421 ± 362 pg/ml, p = .501; between groups T1: p = .404; T2: p = .440) and sCD14 (FFC: 0.346 ± 0.703 vs. 0.175 ± 0.603 μg/ml, p = .509; CFC: 0.336 ± 0.522 vs. 0.546 ± 0.777 μg/ml, p = .587; between groups T1: p = .888; T2: p = .149). CRP was significantly reduced in CFC (0.327 ± 0.449 vs. 0.062 ± 0.231 μg/ml, p = .030) but not in FFC (p = .351). Total-GIS severity during exercise or recovery were not correlated with I-FABP, sCD14, and CRP. The repetitive feeding-challenge with fat, compared with CHO, did not increase markers of gastrointestinal injury, bacterial endotoxin translocation, and systemic inflammation in response to endurance exercise.

articles.title: Comparing the Effects of Water, Sodium-Potassium, and Potassium-Rich Solutions on Fluid Balance and Thermal Strain Following Exercise in the Heat: A Randomized Triple-Blind Crossover Study.
articles.journal: International journal of sport nutrition and exercise metabolism
articles.authors: Joseph A Killick, Elliott J Jenkins, Jemima Benson et al.
articles.abstract: Exercise in the heat perturbs human physiology through elevated core temperature, fluid loss, and cardiovascular strain. While fluid intake can mitigate these effects, the electrolyte composition of hydration solutions may improve rehydration efficacy. This study evaluated whether hydration strategy modulates thermal strain, inflammation, and performance during and after exercise in a hot environment, comparing three different fluid solutions: water, sodium-potassium drink, and coconut water. Twelve participants (seven males) completed a randomized, triple-blind crossover trial. Measures included handgrip strength, countermovement jump, tympanic temperature, thermal sensation, discomfort, body mass, body water percentage, heart rate, and total leukocyte count. Participants were randomly assigned 300 ml of one of three solutions before cycling for 60 min at 1.5 W/kg in ∼33 °C conditions. Additional 300-ml doses were consumed postexercise at 0, 30, and 60 min; measures were taken at each time point before solution consumption and at 90-min postexercise. Following exercise in the heat, a significant main effect for time was observed for all outcomes: thermal responses, heart rate, body mass and body water (p < .001); fatigue (p < .001); and leukocyte count (p = .016), indicating a strong physiological response to heat stress. However, no significant differences were observed between hydration strategies (p ≥ .152) for all measures. In conclusion, exercise in the heat elicited significant thermal strain, fatigue, and inflammation, independent of hydration strategy. Electrolyte composition did not significantly alter responses when fluid intake was controlled, highlighting the need for further research.

articles.title: Seven Days of Highbush Blueberry Supplementation Improves Trail Running Performance in Experienced Runners Without Elevating Physiological or Perceptual Stress Markers.
articles.journal: International journal of sport nutrition and exercise metabolism
articles.authors: Luisa V Giles, Jason P Brandenburg
articles.abstract: Trail running, particularly with a downhill segment, can lead to muscle damage, oxidative stress, and inflammation-factors linked to fatigue. Antioxidant-rich foods like blueberries may help reduce these effects and improve performance. We evaluated 7 days of blueberry supplementation on physiological responses, performance, and recovery from a 22.2-km simulated trail race. Nine runners completed the race following 7 days of freeze-dried blueberry (BLU) and placebo (PLA) powder supplementation. Measurements taken prerace, immediately postrace, and 24 hr postrace included symptoms, pulse wave analysis, pulse wave velocity, reactive strength index, drop jump height, muscle soreness, pulmonary function, salivary cortisol, and immunoglobulin A. Fraction of exhaled nitric oxide was measured pre- and postrace. During the race, heart rate and ratings of perceived exertion for legs and lungs were assessed. Race time was significantly faster with BLU (p = .003), with no differences in race heart rate or ratings of perceived exertion. Supine heart rate (p = .031) and feelings of tiredness (p = .005) were lower in BLU, while FEV1/FVC was higher (p = .023). Drop jump height declined at 24 hr after the trail race in PLA (p = .022) but was preserved in BLU. Blueberry supplementation improved running performance without increasing physiological or perceptual stress.

articles.title: Comparison of 2 Days of Moderate or High Carbohydrate Intake on Physical and Cognitive Performance in Female Team Sport Players During a Simulated Soccer Match Protocol.
articles.journal: International journal of sport nutrition and exercise metabolism
articles.authors: Laura McManus, Michael Scriney, Brendan Egan
articles.abstract: High carbohydrate (CHO) intakes are recommended in the 24-48 hr before soccer matches to increase glycogen stores and delay the development of match-related fatigue, but this concept is unexplored in female soccer players. This study compared the effects of 2 days of divergent CHO intake on physical and cognitive performance during a simulated soccer match protocol. Using a double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover design, 15 female field-based intermittent team sport players consumed either a high CHO diet (6 g·kg body mass [BM]-1·day-1; HIGH) or an isocaloric moderate CHO diet (3 g·kg BM-1·day-1; MOD) for 2 days after completing a standardized (∼35 min) intermittent exercise protocol. For the main experimental trials, participants completed the Loughborough Intermittent Shuttle Test as 5 × 15-min blocks of intermittent running followed by a shuttle run time to exhaustion, with cognitive performance assessed before and after the test. There was no significant difference (6.9 [-71.1, 84.8] s) in time to exhaustion between conditions (HIGH, 295 ± 137 s; MOD, 288 ± 133 s; p = .852; g = 0.05). Sprint times were faster during HIGH compared with MOD at Block 3 (p = .021; g = 0.33), Block 4 (p = .035; g = 0.31), and Block 5 (p < .001; g = 0.34). Rating of perceived exertion was lower during HIGH compared with MOD after Block 1 (p < .001; g = 0.78) and Block 2 (p = .018; g = 0.49). Reaction time in the Task Switching test was improved from pre- to postexercise in HIGH (p = .017; g = 0.67) but not MOD (p = .913; g = 0.05). These results suggest that female soccer players may benefit from increasing daily CHO intake to at least 6 g/kg BM for the 2 days preceding competitive matches.
